SAN JOSE, Calif. (CN) â A federal judge ruled Monday that the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has six months to make a final decision on listing the California spotted owl for protection under the Endangered Species Act, after several years of delays prompted the Center for Biological Diversity to sue the service.

U.S. District Judge Eumi K. Lee considered a basic question in granting in part the centerâs motion for summary judgment: âBy what date should the court order [Fish and Wildlife] to satisfy its statutory duty to issue a final listing determination for the California spotted owl?â she noted in her 16-page ruling.

Lee, a Joe Biden appointee, landed on April 30, 2027, far later than Nov. 19, 2026, the date the center, an environmental nonprofit that often sues government agencies to advance protections for vulnerable species, had originally suggested.

âWhether FWS should be able to satisfy its statutory obligation in less than a month does not indicate that FWS is able to do so as a matter of fact,â Lee wrote. âBecause there is no indication that a final rule submitted in less than thirty days from this order would withstand future judicial scrutiny, ordering such rapid relief may be self-defeating.â

Still, the six-month deadline is sooner than the proposed date of May 10, 2028, the service argued was the soonest it would be able to make a final listing determination for the owl, citing budget constraints and a workload made heavier by a settlement with the center that requires the service to make final listing determinations for 76 species in the next four years.

âFWS first contends that completing the final listing determination for the California spotted owl before May 10, 2028, is infeasible because of the agencyâs resources and existing court-ordered deadlines,â Lee wrote. âThe court is not persuaded.â

As part of the settlement with the service, the center agreed not to sue the service over missed Endangered Species Act statutory deadlines for no more than two species per fiscal year, and only âif the center determines that the species faces an imminent risk of extinction.â The center sued the service over the California spotted owlâs final listing determination in November 2025.

The California spotted owl is a raptor species that has been in need of protection for over two decades, the center said, because its habitat is old-growth forests in the Sierra Nevada and its small populations in Central and Southern California are threatened by human encroachment andÂ logging.

âThe current administration has launched a full-scale attack on Americaâs national forests,â Greg Loarie, Earthjustice attorney representing the center, said in an email to Courthouse News. âThis ruling gives us hope that the California spotted owl will receive the protection it so urgently needs to survive the assault and one day recover.â

At a hearing for the motion on Oct. 28, the service said it would need more time to address 50 public comments made in 2023 about the owlâs proposed listing but didnât say how much time it would need. Lee said in her order that six months should be enough time to go through the comments and complete an internal review for approval.

MANASSAS, Va. (CN) â Months before her disappearance, Mamta Kafle Bhatt made an admission about her relationship with her husband during a phone call with her brother: “I am not safe.”

Her brother’s testimony Monday wrapped up the prosecution’s case against her husband, Naresh Bhatt. Over four weeks of testimony, prosecutors sought to persuade a jury that Naresh Bhatt, 39, murdered his 28-year-old wife.

Naresh Bhatt has pleaded not guilty. The Manassas Park man’s legal team asserts the prosecution lacks evidence: Mamta Bhatt’s body was never found.

But prosecutors say the woman did not just leave her home and abandon her infant daughter. Instead, they contend Naresh Bhatt killed his wife, dismembered her body and disposed of her remains in area trash dumpsters.

Taking the stand as the final witness for the prosecution, Mamta Bhatt’s brother, Mahesh Kafle, recounted a conversation in which his sister said she was mistreated. Speaking with the aid of an interpreter, Kafle, who is from Nepal, recalled that his sister asked him to save a photo that showed her with facial bruises.

Years before, when she first announced she was going to marry, her brother met Naresh Bhatt and was negatively impressed. “I told her not to get married to this man,” Kafle testified.

Mandira Shrestha, a longtime friend of Naresh Bhatt, also testified for the prosecution. She recalled that after Mamta Bhatt vanished, Naresh Bhatt wanted Shrestha to take back a piece of jewelry she’d given to Mamta.

“He asked me to come and collect it because it was mine,” she said, testifying through an interpreter. When Shrestha arrived, Naresh Bhatt decided to give away more: “All of Mamta’s jewelry â and also his ring, his chain. All the jewelry they had.”

When she asked why, Bhatt said his mother told him to. “There are a lot of people coming in and out of the house, and it will be safe,” Shrestha testified. If Mamta Bhatt returned, she was told she could return the jewelry. Otherwise, she should give it to Mamta’s mother. Shrestha eventually gave it to the police.

Shrestha also testified Bhatt asked her to adopt the couple’s daughter. Mamta Bhatt’s brother is raising the child.

Prosecutors left the jury with images of Mamta Bhatt as a healthy young woman, including a video in which she sang a children’s song with her infant daughter. Another video showed the couple embracing. Watching from his seat at the defense table, Naresh Bhatt wept.

DNA testimony linking the young woman to suspected blood stains discovered in the house was also part of the day’s testimony. Forensic analysts testified about evidence gathered by crime scene investigators using Bluestar, a chemical that detects the presence of old or cleaned-up blood. After spraying the bathroom, blue spots glowed around the tub and in front of the shower, indicating a past suspected bloodstain. Investigators found more evidence of a possible stain in the bedroom carpet.

Defense attorneys pushed back, pointing out investigators actually gathered the evidence. Forensic analysts were involved later in the process. Naresh Bhatt’s legal team is expected to rebut this evidence by targeting crime scene techniques used by police and will begin its case Wednesday.

In the 1983 movie A Christmas Story, Ralphie’s teacher, Miss Shields, assigns her students the task of writing “a theme.” The fourth-grade class at Warren G. Harding Elementary school erupts in groans; after all, writing is hard work.

But Ralphie sees it as an opportunity to make his case for a Red Ryder BB gun, “the Holy Grail of Christmas gifts.” And as the words “pour[] forth from [his] penny pencil with feverish fluidity,” he gets right to the point: “What I want for Christmas is a Red Ryder BB gun with a compass in the stock and this thing that tells time.”

Doubtless, Miss Shields had admonished her students – like our teachers admonished us – that each paragraph of a theme must begin with a thesis (or topic) sentence. But is that always right? Pay attention to skilled writers, and you’ll discover that – like many things – it depends.

Skilled writers do locate a paragraph’s issue (topic) and its point (thesis) where readers expect to encounter them. But readers have different expectations about where that should be. Sometimes readers expect the issue and the point in the first sentence, but sometimes they expect them to be separated. Readers change their expectations depending on what type of paragraph they are reading. And sometimes a paragraph has no point at all.

Justice Elena Kagan shows how this works. She never makes a reader hunt for her point, even though she might locate that point in different places for different types of paragraphs.

Take Smith & Wesson v. Estados Unidos Mexicanos as one of many potential examples. In Smith & Wesson, the court held that Mexico had failed to plead its way around a federal statute barring claims against gun manufacturers. Starting with meat-and-potatoes paragraphs, Kagan does exactly what Miss Shields might insist upon. She locates both the issue and the point of the paragraph right at the beginning, then uses the rest of the paragraph to prove her point.

In Section I.A. of the opinion, for example, Kagan sets out the requirements of the statute being interpreted, the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act. Taking only the first sentence of each paragraph, readers learn exactly how the statute works with zero effort. We read:

“[The PLCAA] bars cer­tain lawsuits against manufacturers and sellers of fire­arms.”

“But PLCAA’s general bar on those suits has an exception, usually called the predicate exception, relevant here.”

“Notably here, the predicate violation PLCAA demands may come from aiding and abetting someone else’s firearms offense.”

After each thesis, Kagan deploys the PLCAA’s language to prove that she’s right. For example, to prove that the PLCAA “bars certain lawsuits,” she quotes language providing that a “qualified civil liability action . . . may not be brought in any Federal or State court.” But again, before she shoves the reader’s nose into the language, she first tells us the point of it all.

In adopting this structure, Kagan is giving English readers what they expect. In his book “The Sense of Structure,” George Gopen calls these meat-and-potatoes paragraphs “medial paragraphs.” Here, in the middle of an exposition, “readers tend to appreciate being given the point up front.” Fail to put the point up front and one risks “having the reader disappear before the point actually arrives.” You run an especially grave risk if you are writing for busy legal readers – an audience that’s typically looking for a reason to stop reading.

But in other types of paragraphs, Kagan does not front-load a traditional thesis sentence, and she’s right there too. Consider the way Kagan writes introductions and narrative paragraphs.

In her Smith & Wesson introduction, Kagan reveals the issue or the topic in the first sentence, but she only gives the point or thesis in the last sentence. In the first sentence, we read that Mexico has sued American gun manufacturers – what the case is about. But before we can understand the court’s holding – the point – we need to learn some context. We need a sketch of what the law requires. So Kagan next sets out the statutory requirement: Mexico must plead that the gun manufacturers aided and abetted unlawful sales to the cartels. Only now, at the end of the paragraph, do we know enough to understand the point: Mexico did not plausibly plead aiding and abetting.

Again, according to Gopen, Kagan is satisfying her readers’ “remarkably fixed expectation that the point of an opening paragraph will arrive at the end.” We readers don’t want to be punched in the face with an answer before we know enough to understand it. Writers should make us “comfortable with the surroundings before we have to go to work.”

Narrative paragraphs involve yet another difference: readers don’t expect a traditional thesis in a passage that feels like “once upon a time.” Gopen notes, “Not all paragraphs were born to make a point.” Sometimes writers write “just to tell a story, to put some facts on the table.”

In her narrative paragraphs, Kagan sometimes just tells the story, and sometimes she fires a thesis point blank:

In the end, your old English teacher was mostly right. Ordinary, meat-and-potatoes paragraphs ought to have a sentence in which the issue and the point are together at the beginning of the paragraph. But specialized paragraphs might be different. So, before you start line-editing the sentences of a draft, employ a process to evaluate the strength of your paragraphs.

For your meat-and-potatoes paragraphs, prefer paragraphs that state the point and then prove it. Be on the lookout for paragraphs that write to a conclusion rather than stating it up front. To diagnose these paragraphs, try to create a reverse outline by copying the first sentence (sometimes two) into a different document. Ask yourself whether the argument makes sense with only those sentences. It will if the issue and point are stated up front.

In your statement of facts, mark which paragraphs have a thesis and which don’t. Know that you have a choice about when to include one, and make that choice.

Finally, give special attention to paragraphs that begin a text or a new section. Take the reader from the issue, through the necessary context, and then conclude with the point.

Why so much care? Because hitting the wrong target can be dangerous; you’ll shoot your eye out. A legal reader won’t just stand by trying to guess where the next round is being aimed.

Correction (Nov. 2 at 5:00 p.m.): A prior version of this article gave the case name as Smith & Wesson v. Estados Unidos de Mexico.

Professor Gray teaches legal writing courses for first-year and advanced students at Duke Law.

#7578. California city fends off data center developer’s sabotage claims

A developer said the city illegally took several actions to prevent its data center plans for 194 acres in California's Imperial Valley. A federal judge wasn't convinced by the claims.

(CN) â A federal judge on Monday threw out a developer’s lawsuit, in which it claimed the city of Imperial impeded its plan for three contiguous data centers on 194 acres in southeastern California.

U.S. District Judge Janis Sammartino dismissed every claim brought by Imperial Valley Computer Manufacturing, known as IVCM, against the city and its officials. The judge, however, granted the company leave to amend its complaint.

The company accused the city of denying it a fair process, treating it worse than similar developers and retaliating against it.

The land spans the city of Imperial, Imperial County and El Centro, near the U.S.-Mexico border. The company said the city got in the way of its plans by insisting on its own discretionary review and ignoring deadlines.

The developer also claimed the $10 billion projectwould have brought 1,688 construction jobs and 100 permanent jobs to the Imperial Valley.

The cityâs community development director, Ohtan Mora, denied the companyâs first site plan in July 2025 and said it needed an environmental assessment and a zoning change. He rejected a second application, and the company withdrew it the next day.

After City Manager Dennis Morita told the company a public review process was necessary, it moved the project to county land. The developer says the city then âlaunched a coordinated campaign to sabotage the data center.â

Sammartino found the company’s fair-process claim fell apart, because it had a way to challenge the cityâs decision and didnât use it. It could have appealed to the cityâs planning commission and then sought judicial review in state court.

âIVCM may not abandon its application and then claim it was denied due process,â the George Bush appointee wrote.

IVCM argued the city missed a 15-day deadline to act, so its plans were automatically approved. Sammartino said that did not give the company a constitutional right to approval, because the cityâs zoning code gives the planning director discretion over site plan applications.

The company said the city treated its plans differently from other industrial projects. Sammartino disagreed. She noted the company pointed to developments like warehouses, food banks and fertilizer makers â not other data centers.

âThe court finds it rational that defendants would decide to treat a 675,000 square foot data center differently than a 289,000 square foot warehouse,â she wrote.

She said the company could amend that claim.

âIt is possible that sufficiently similar comparators exist in the city,â she wrote. âBut IVCM has not alleged them here.â

The company’s retaliation claims involved several actions, including the city’s review process, public statements and a lawsuit the city filed against Imperial County in December 2025. The city had asked a judge to undo the countyâs grading permit for the project. The company called the lawsuit a sham.

Sammartino found the company’s claims about the city’s review process, interference with a water agreement and public statements did not sufficiently prove those actions would discourage an ordinary person from exercising their First Amendment rights.

Sammartino did find the lawsuit could have had a chilling effect, but said the company still needed to show the city filed it in retaliation.

A California Superior Court granted the city’s petition in September, finding the county’s grading permit was not a ministerial approval that officials had to issue automatically. Sammartino said she did not need to agree with the merits of that ruling. As the city had prevailed in state court, she found it had probable cause to bring the lawsuit.

She added that the First Amendment also protects the right to take a complaint to court, shielding the city’s lawsuit from the company’s retaliation claim.

IVCM claimed Councilmember Katherine Burnworth and the local nonprofit Comite Civico del Valle shared an aim: to create âleverage necessary for CCV to demand a settlement.â

âAlthough improper, this motive is not retaliation,â Sammartino wrote.

She also noted the companyâs complaint spends 35 paragraphs on the Imperial Irrigation Districtâs actions.

âHowever, IID is not a defendant in this lawsuit,â she wrote.

Sammartino found some parts of the company’s claims plausible, but ultimately dismissed all the claims, including the company’s claim seeking to hold the city liable for its officials’ conduct.

The company must amend its claims within 30 days.

Representatives for IVCM and the city of Imperial didnât immediately respond to requests for comment.

#7576. Is Montgomery affirmative action’s final chapter?

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

On Oct. 19, the Supreme Court granted cert in a case called Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education. I am surprised it hasn’t received more press coverage because it could be the final nail in affirmative action’s coffin.

Perhaps you think the Supreme Court already hammered in that nail in Students for Fair Admissions, Inc. v. President & Fellows of Harvard College, but you’d be wrong. In that case, the court found racial preferences at Harvard and the University of North Carolina to be illegal. Nevertheless, many scholars are now urging schools to turn to what I call “race neutral affirmative action.” These are programs that seek to increase the number of some racial groups relative to others not by selecting for race itself, but by selecting for characteristics correlated with race. For example, instead of using race preferences in admissions, a university uses preferences for applicants who live in zip codes that are nearly all black, applicants who grew up on Indian reservations, or applicants for whom English is a second language. These are real-life examples of what some universities have done when they were forbidden from using race. Many affirmative action supporters think these sorts of things are perfectly legal.

But I have long argued that race proxies are just as illegal as using race itself. My arguments became moot points after the Supreme Court allowed universities to use race itself in admissions in the 2003 case of Grutter v. Bollinger. But now that SFFA has taken that off the table, the question I teed up is back in the limelight: is it constitutional to use racial proxies instead?

That’s what Montgomery County allegedly did to pick the students for its magnet middle schools. Its efforts predated SFFA because, even before the Supreme Court told universities not to use race, they had told school districts not to. In a nutshell, the alleged facts are these: Asian children make up only 15% of the school system’s population – it is majority black and Hispanic – but were taking up half the spots in the magnet middle schools. This didn’t go over well with many parents, so the school board sought to even things out. The board tried several plans but ultimately used a lottery among the applicants who scored above the 85th percentile in their neighborhood on standardized tests. Because the pool was based on how well applicants did compared only to others in their own neighborhood, the plan spread magnet school spots across the county – and, because many neighborhoods don’t have much racial diversity, it spread the spots across the races, too. The number of black and Latino students went up and the number of Asian students went down.

According to Supreme Court precedent, this is unconstitutional. We have a long history of attempts to discriminate indirectly when we couldn’t discriminate directly – and we have an equally long history of the Supreme Court telling us it’s illegal. For example, when we couldn’t deny the ability to vote on the basis of race, we tried using literacy tests and grandfather clauses and felon disenfranchisement instead. The court said those things are illegal. When we couldn’t segregate schools, we tried drawing school district boundaries around mostly black neighborhoods and mostly white neighborhoods instead. The court said we can’t do that, either.

The doctrine is this: if your “purpose” is to discriminate on the basis of race and your “effect” is to discriminate on the basis of race, then you are engaged in discrimination on the basis of race – even if you aren’t using a racial classification. It’s something like the old adage: if something walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it’s a duck.

Most scholars supported these precedents when people were discriminating against blacks. But now not so much. Thus, I expect a bevy of amicus briefs from academics contorting their way through them. But the contortions I have seen thus far are very weak. For example, the leading theory on why these precedents don’t doom Montgomery County is the old distinction between “benign” and “invidious” discrimination: the purpose to help is different than the purpose to hurt. The precedents involved the purpose to hurt blacks, whereas Montgomery County was trying to help blacks (and Latinos); hurting Asians was just a byproduct, not the purpose.

If you thought the Supreme Court had already rejected – over and over again – the distinction between “benign” and “invidious” discrimination, you’d be right. After all, that’s how we got SFFA. As the court explained there, life is often zero-sum: if you help one race by giving them more spots, you necessarily hurt other races by giving them fewer spots. What is “benign” for one is “invidious” for the others. It’s a distinction without a difference.

The scholars say the cases rejecting the benign-invidious distinction don’t count because they involved racial classifications, not racial proxies. But the court in SFFA anticipated this move and cut it off: “[U]niversities may not simply establish through . . . other means the regime we hold unlawful today. … [W]hat cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly. … The Constitution deals with substance, not shadows.” Yes, that’s dicta, but isn’t it very, very probative of what the very same justices will think about the very same question next year?

Moreover, the dicta didn’t come from nowhere: in fact, the Supreme Court has already struck down “benign” racial proxies – a bunch of them. When governments engage in racial gerrymandering of voting districts, they don’t use racial classifications: voters are assigned to one district or another based on where they live, not their skin color. Yet, even when these gerrymanders have been designed to help black and Latino voters, the Supreme Court has struck them down all the same, including just this past term in Louisiana v. Callais. Is not Montgomery County engaged in gerrymandering no less than Louisiana? It’s just school districts, not voting districts.

It is true that the court has required discriminators to try “race-neutral alternatives” before they can use race itself. But the court requires race-neutral alternatives only when discriminators otherwise have a compelling interest to justify their discrimination. All this means is that the court prefers racial proxies to racial classifications when forced to choose; it doesn’t mean racial proxies are insulated from constitutional scrutiny.

Still, the court may not need to get into all this because the question presented in the Montgomery County case merely asks what counts as a discriminatory “effect.” The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit held that the Asian students had to show a “disparate impact” – a term borrowed from Title VII law that means the challenged practice impacts one race more than another – and they couldn’t do so because, even after the gerrymandering, they still comprised a greater portion of the magnet school spots than they did of magnet school applicants.

Although it is true that disparate impact is one way to show a racial effect under the Supreme Court’s purpose-and-effect precedents, as I previously explained, it is not the only way. For example, when the Supreme Court said that school districts couldn’t evade its desegregation decrees by drawing district lines around mostly white neighborhoods and mostly black neighborhoods, it did not require the plaintiffs to show a disparate impact (e.g., schools of different quality); it was enough that one school was overwhelmingly white and the other was overwhelmingly black. When the Supreme Court has said that legislatures couldn’t gerrymander voting districts, it did not require the plaintiffs to show a disparate impact (e.g., differential vote dilution); it was enough that the racial composition of the districts had been affected.

It is true that what exactly the racial effect is in the voting cases is undertheorized. There is no obvious baseline to compare to the gerrymandered district lines in order to measure the “effect.” For this reason, some scholars think the court has all but read out the effect requirement from the purpose-and-effect test. Maybe so. The effect requirement comes from an old case called Palmer v. Thompson: there, Jackson, Mississippi, closed all their public swimming pools rather than desegregate them; the court held that this wasn’t unconstitutional racial discrimination because all the races had been affected equally. The ruling is unpopular among scholars on the left; law professor Randall Kennedy at Harvard has compared it to Korematsu. Thus, I doubt many will mourn its demise; plaintiffs would still have to show an injury to establish standing in federal court. But overruling it will only help the plaintiffs in the Montgomery County case.

Still, a lingering question that hasn’t been asked enough is whether the purpose-and-effect doctrine – or even a purpose-only doctrine if Palmer goes away – is consistent with the original understanding of the Constitution. It is hard for me to see how it couldn’t be: it is very easy to evade any rule by proxy; surely, they knew that even back in 1868. But I haven’t seen any historical analyses yet. I hope there are some in the briefing.

I appreciate that for many scholars it is inconceivable that we could end up in a world where it is illegal to do anything about racial disparities. Many of them endorse so-called “antiracism” and believe that all racial disparities must be the product of racism – and, indeed, that we, too, are racists if we don’t do something about them. This means we can sometimes have “too many” Asians. Maybe they’re right about that, maybe they’re wrong. But the 14th Amendment does not enact Mr. Ibram X. Kendi’s “How to Be an Antiracist.”

Brian Fitzpatrick was a law clerk to Antonin Scalia and is currently the Milton R. Underwood Chair in Free Enterprise and Professor of Law at Vanderbilt Law School.

CHULA VISTA, Calif. (CN) â A San Diego Superior Court judge Monday sentenced Larry Millete to 25 years to life in prison on Monday after an emotional day in court as family members of Maya Millete recalled their memories of a mother, aunt and sister.

A jury convicted Larry Millete in July of murdering Maya Millete, who was last seen at her Chula Vista home on Jan. 7, 2021. Her body has never been found.

The sentencing followed two hours of victim impact statements from family members who pleaded with the convicted murderer to reveal the location of Maya Millete’s remains.

âThe search consumes our lives,â Maricris Drouaillet, Maya Millete’s oldest sister and legal guardian of her children, told the court. âI hope he finds peace, and I hope it brings him a change of heart and he tells us where my sister is so we can lay her to rest. Maya deserves to come home. We hope that one day our family can find some peace again.â

Although her remains were not recovered, prosecutors established a case based on circumstantial evidence that showed the coupleâs marriage had been in trouble and Larry had been controlling, abusive and obsessed.

He repeatedly purchased online spells to regain his wifeâs affection or to sicken and injure her, prosecutors said. They also presented evidence that he turned off his phone and left his residence for about 12 hours, driving about 444 miles in his vehicle the morning after Maya Millete was last seen.

Family members expressed feeling betrayed by someone they had seen as a family member.

Speaking for the first time, the coupleâs two teenage daughters, Maylani and Lara Millete, also asked their father to reveal where their motherâs body was.

âI find myself and my siblings to be stuck in a very complicated position,â Lara told the courtroom. âI am the daughter of the victim and simultaneously the daughter of the defendant."

“As his daughter, I cannot stop loving him,” she continued. “He is the only parent we have left.â

Larry Millete also addressed the courtroom, insisting he was not a bad person and describing himself as a loving father.

“I am not a monster,” he said. âI just hope one day I can make amends and reconcile. Time does heal all wounds."

Millete has long denied killing his wife.

âMy only regret is that I wasnât able to protect my wife enough,â he said. âShe wasn’t just my wife, she was my best friend.â

He also told each of his children that he loved them and was proud of them. However, tensions boiled over when he addressed Maya Millete’s other family members.

âI know itâs hard to believe, but I really love your sister,â he told her brother, who shook his head. âIt’s hard being without her.â

âThen why did you kill her?â Maya Millete’s niece, Rica Casino, shouted from across the courtroom before rushing toward him and being restrained by other family members.

Presiding Superior Court Judge Enrique Camarena, Jr. also allowed Larry Millete’s family to speak in support of him.

“I am not ashamed of you,” his mother, Judith Millete, said. “I am proud of you because you did not murder anybody.”

Hi father Benito Millete also defended his son and even went so far as to accuse Maya Millete of having a drinking problem.

Deputy District Attorney Christy Bowles objected to these statements, but Benito Millete appeared to suffer from a medical episode and was removed from court.

âThe record before the court does not demonstrate humility or responsibility,â he said of Larry Millete. âHe has maintained a posture of denial and defiance. Of particular gravity is the defendantâs callousness in the immediate aftermath of the murder.â

The evidence also showed Millete was uninterested in helping locate his missing wife, the judge said.

âFrankly the court finds the conduct abhorrent,â he said.

Camarena also granted a protective order prohibiting contact between Millete and his children. The children could seek to modify the order once they become adults, he ruled.

Milleteâs defense attorneys requested a new trial based on purported juror misconduct, statements made to the media and evidentiary concerns. Camarena denied the request.

San Diego District Attorney Summer Stephan congratulated prosecutors and law enforcement for securing a conviction and significant prison sentence.

âThis case is about deadly control,â Stephan told reporters after the sentencing. âIf Larry Millete could not have Maya, no one in the world would ever get to enjoy her company, including her three children and loving family. This murder conviction and sentence finally holds Larry Millete accountable, for the cruel murder he committed, taking the life of this mother.â

Deputy District Attorney Christy Bowles said it was “the privilege of my life to be a voice for Maya Millete and advocate for justice on behalf of her family and friends.”

âBut this case is an absolute tragedy," Bowles said. “So many people have suffered as a result of the defendant’s actions in this case, and no one more than his children. It is my sincere hope that one day, we can bring closure to them and bring their mother home so they can lay her to rest.â

#7572. Supreme Court declines Trump administration's request to intervene in California ballot dispute

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Trump administration on Monday morning asked the Supreme Court to intervene in its efforts to keep California from counting ballots cast by what it contends are more than 20,000 noncitizens who have registered to vote in that state. In a brief, unsigned order released to reporters shortly before 6 p.m., however, the court turned down the government's request. There were no noted dissents.

In a 19-page filing, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer requested an order from the justices that would require California to keep those ballots separate until the voters’ citizenship could be verified. “Once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones,” Sauer wrote, “there is no way to get the challenged ballots back.”

The filing was the latest chapter in the Trump administration’s push to combat alleged voter fraud. It began last month, when the administration went to federal court in Los Angeles, seeking an order directing the state not to send ballots to, or count the ballots of, voters who were likely not citizens.

On Oct. 28, U.S. District Judge David Carter turned down the government’s request for a temporary order directing California to sequester the ballots of “likely noncitizens.” Among other things, he questioned the credibility of the Trump administration’s allegations that the voters it had identified were not U.S. citizens. On Friday, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit also rejected the Trump administration’s motion for emergency relief.

With the midterm elections now just one day away, the Trump administration sought relief next in the Supreme Court. Sauer argued that the government is likely to prevail on the merits of its claim – a key factor that courts consider in deciding whether to grant temporary relief – because federal law bars anyone who is not a U.S. citizen from voting in federal elections. Therefore, he wrote, “it follows that any ballot cast by an alien is unlawful” and states cannot count them.

The United States will also suffer permanent harm (another factor that courts consider in deciding whether to award temporary relief), Sauer continued, because “‘California admits that there is no way to trace a ballot after it is processed.’” The government’s “injury will continue to mount,” Sauer contended, “through Tuesday, November 10 (a week after election day, California’s deadline for receiving mail ballots.)”

By contrast, Sauer said, California will not suffer “undue hardship” from having to sequester the ballots at issue in this case. Indeed, he suggested, “California’s own election laws contemplate the segregation of challenged ballots, and the segregation of challenged ballots is a standard remedy in election cases.”

Sauer asked the court to also issue an immediate temporary order, known as an administrative injunction, “that requires California to segregate mail ballots from persons whom the United States has identified as likely noncitizens” while the justices consider the government’s request.

The Trump administration’s filing went first to Justice Elena Kagan, who has primary responsibility for emergency appeals from the 9th Circuit. Kagan then referred it to the full court, which declined the Trump administration’s request.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

Ignition is one of the oldest Apple Technical Partners on the planet, and the only fractional IT firm that specializes in the venture-backed technology ecosystem.

Fully Remote · Work from home · Full-time (Eastern or Pacific time zones) · Apple-first

ignitionit.com is a seasoned, Apple-first MSP — in business for almost 30 years — and we're hiring a Help Desk Technician to be the friendly, capable first voice our clients reach when something isn't working. This position is a remote, work-from-home, full-time role.

We've written this as a junior-to-mid-level job description because that's where most great people start on our team. But if you're more seasoned — comfortable in identity, MDM, or security work — don't scroll past. We'd be delighted to find someone who can step in higher up the ladder, and we'll happily talk about a more senior scope and comp if that's you.

Unlike many IT shops, we believe that the technology is the tactic. The actual job is making people feel taken care of. One of our core values is “49% tech support, 51% human support.”

You'll succeed by configuring devices, resetting access, untangling email, and chasing down the gremlin that's been haunting someone's conference room. But you'll know you succeeded when a client exhales and says, “Thank goodness you're on it!” That Warm Fuzzy Feeling™ is the actual product. The green lights on the dashboard are just how we get there.

Onboard a new hire at a fast-growing startup: provision their Mac, set up their Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 accounts, enroll the device in MDM, and make sure day one feels effortless.

Offboard a departing employee cleanly — recover the laptop, revoke access, and close the loop so nothing's left dangling. All boxes checked, ticket notated and closed, client followed up with.

Field a "my email stopped working" ticket that turns out to be a DNS thing, a phishing-filter thing, or a "they changed their password on their phone three weeks ago" thing.

Help a family office or RIA get a touchy Zoom Room or conference-room AV setup behaving before a meeting — over the phone.

Triage the queue so phones get answered fast, emails don't rot, and nobody feels forgotten — even when the honest answer is, “We're on it, but here's the realistic timeline."

⠀ You'll be the front line: helping with what you can, researching what you can't, and pinging the rest of the team when you're genuinely stuck. That last part is a skill, not a weakness — knowing when to ask is half the job.

We're one of the oldest Apple Technical Partners on the planet, and one of the only certified Apple Premier Partners — that’s kinda like getting knighted by the ghost of Steve Jobs. We started where you’d expect to find Macs (creative agencies, non-profits, education) but our primary clients today are cutting-edge, venture-backed AI SaaS startups, VC and private equity firms, registered investment advisors — many of them operating under stringent compliance expectations (SOC 2, SEC). That means we hold ourselves to a higher standard than the scrappy shop we started as. Polished, reliable, security-minded work is the baseline now — but always with a smile!

What hasn't changed: relationships are still our most valuable currency — with clients, with vendors, and with each other. We're a tight, supportive team. We teach each other what we know, cover for each other when life throws a punch, and care a little too much about doing things the right way. We're still a bit weird, and our clients seem to like us that way.

We move fast, priorities shift, it’s not always documented (whatever it is), our tool set and list of supported platforms is sprawling, and some days the to-do list is longer than you'd like. If you can stay warm under pressure, create order out of chaos, learn new stuff fast because you love it, and speak up when you need help, you'll thrive here.

If you need a rigid, fully-documented, never-changes environment where nobody trusts you with admin access, where you will be micro-managed so you never have to wonder whether or not you’re doing the right thing, this isn't it. You’ll have a ton of independence on our team, and freedom to use your best judgment to get the ball over the finish line, but that also means we expect you to be naturally responsible, honest, and highly accountable — to yourself, your teammates, and the clients. As they say, the price of freedom is eternal vigilance.

Apple at the core — macOS, iOS, Apple Business Manager, and MDM (Jamf / Iru / Intune / Workspace ONE / and more)

#7565. Instagram is offering YouTubers up to $500,000 to post with its new horizontal format

Instagram isn’t just chasing YouTube‘s TV watch time and ad revenue–it’s chasing its talent, too. The Meta-owned platform has offered to pay some YouTubers up to $500,000 to post videos with its newly announced long-form horizontal format “Features.”

According to Business Insider, Instagram has approached “select” YouTubers with a floor price of $50,000; others have gotten six-figure offers, and things top out at a half-million dollars.

“We’ve been public about the fact that we are funding Features content directly with some creators right now to support them,” a Meta spokesperson told BI. “The details of those deals are confidential, but we’re excited to see the content going live.”

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

It’s not clear how Instagram is paying out these amounts–per video, per month, or as one-time flat compensation. We’d bet the latter, and perhaps the pot’s sweetened with a promise to pay creators performance bonuses or an ad rev share if their Features content does well (especially on TVs, where pricier ads slots can pull in serious cash for platforms).

Meta already said, though, that it’s “too early to share a long-term monetization model [for Features], but we’re exploring ways for creators to earn from brands, fans, and Instagram, including performance-based incentives.”

Introducing Features earlier this week, Instagram hyped its established TV viewership, with VP of Product Tessa Lyons saying “people love to watch Reels together in their living rooms with their friends, so we’ve been working on a TV version of Reels.”

“[W]e know to do that well, we need more than just short-form video,” she added.

Insta chief Adam Mosseri chimed in Oct. 28 after concern from creators, tweeting that “[w]e understand the economics matter a ton, and are exploring multiple options to help long-form creators get paid.”

This YouTuber-bait program is perhaps one of those options.

People familiar with the deals told BI Instagram’s terms just ask creators to post their long-form videos as Features on the same day they upload to YouTube.

Reza Izad, who reps Kareem Rahma, Noah Beck, and more as co-founder and co-CEO of Underscore Talent, told BI these deals are an “exciting opportunity” for YouTubers. The money is part of that excitement, sure, but Izad said this is also an opportunity for creators’ content to get a boost.

“Every time there’s a new feature in these apps that the company’s promoting, people will have more opportunity to be seen because there’s going to be algorithmic preference to this kind of content,” he said. “And unlike short-form, there’s not a lot of abundance.”

What he’s saying is true: We already know Instagram plans to pump posts made with Clips as Reels (a tool that takes snippets of Features videos and posts them to Reels with a link back to the full long-form upload) on its Explore page, and in other areas around the platform.

Something to think about in all of this is that a major part of YouTube’s living room success is the relative attractiveness and easy UX of its TV app. Google has put stock into making the TV app a banger, and Instagram isn’t there yet.

As Mosseri put it, “We’re going to try to support these different types of formats, both in the mobile app, but also on the TV app, which […] is going to take some time to get it right. But I’m actually very excited about it, and we’re very committed to it long-term.”

Creators looking for equal viewership across YouTube and Features will likely be disappointed–at least for now. But for the folks Instagram wants to pay, this is indeed a rare chance to get get cash for cross-posting.

#7561. ‘E’ For ‘Exactly The Same As Always’; Google’s Very Bad Day On Wall Street

An academic study co-authored by researchers at Indiana University and New Jersey Institute of Technology, working with ad tech research firms Adalytics and DeepSee.io, raises serious concerns about the misuse of extended identifiers (EIDs) in programmatic advertising.

EIDs are persistent user identifiers, such as hashed email addresses, that are used to link and track users across different domains and devices.

The study found that ad tech companies were attaching real human tracking data to automated internet bots, falsely making it look like real people were visiting certain sites. In some instances, they even bundled multiple different human IDs into a single bot session or advertising bid.

Zeta Global’s LiveIntent was singled out for particularly brazen behavior, as per Jack Neff’s writeup on the study. Criteo, ID5 and Experian’s Audigent were also observed assigning different EIDs to separate supply paths in multi-SSP auctions.

Flashtalking, however, received a gold star, as it was the only one out of 18 ad tech vendors that was never documented serving human EIDs to bots. The Trade Desk, meanwhile, came close, keeping its hands almost entirely clean.

It’s worth noting that the practice doesn’t qualify as sophisticated invalid traffic under the Media Rating Council’s standards. And, as a spokesperson from the MRC tells Neff, the organization “does not currently audit or accredit any identity solutions/providers nor audience targeting.”

Google may consider itself an AI company these days, but as far as investors are concerned, it’s still mainly an advertising business.

The share price for Google’s parent company Alphabet dropped roughly 13% yesterday after its Q3 earnings call on Wednesday. It was the worst day for Alphabet’s stock since the company went public in 2004, according to The Wall Street Journal.

It was softness in Google’s search ads business that spooked investors, the FT reports.

During the earnings call, an investor pointed out that Google’s search revenue growth had gradually slowed this year. It went from 19% in Q1 to 17% in Q2 and 12% in Q3.

This observation prompted Google’s chief business officer, Philipp Schindler, to confirm that “the strong growth in AI Mode queries had an impact because of the lower monetization we were seeing in AI Mode.”

In other words, Google’s AI search business isn’t just making less money than traditional search; it’s actually dragging down Google’s search revenue. Cue the investor panic.

“In a market worried about AI chatbots cannibalizing [Google’s] key franchise, investors need to see [search] accelerating, not decelerating,” David Wagner at Aptus Capital Advisors tells the FT.

But Google is betting that by cannibalizing one of its strongest revenue lines in the short term, it’ll achieve even greater growth later on – after it loads up AI search with ads, that is.

These days, sports coverage can make or break a media company’s earnings report card.

TelevisaUnivision reported a 14% drop in US revenue during the third quarter, and US advertising revenue in particular tanked 24%. Ruh-roh.

The Spanish-language media giant faced tough competition for viewers and advertisers last quarter, given that its rival Telemundo had snagged Spanish-language US rights to cover the 2026 FIFA World Cup. But it’s not all doom and gloom for TelevisaUnivision, which luckily had airing rights to the tournament in Latin America via its TV network and streaming service, ViX.

TelevisaUnivision credits its LATAM World Cup coverage for a 30% increase in overall subscription and licensing revenue, with Mexico proving to be an especially valuable tailwind. The company’s quarterly revenue rose 51% in the region, and ad revenue spiked 19%.

Those gains somewhat offset steeper losses in the US, with TelevisaUnivision’s overall ad revenue declining by an average of 5% last quarter (a far more palatable number than 24%).

Going forward, company executives told investors that the plan is to continue growing audience reach across linear and streaming platforms – which, predictably, includes expanding its sports portfolio.

WPP’s revenue was down 2.1% in Q3, but WPP Media saw positive growth for the first time in six quarters, at 0.3%. WPP CEO Cindy Rose details how the holdco’s priorities have changed since she took the helm last year. [Adweek]

Health, food and news publishers have suffered the steepest declines in organic search traffic over the past two years – but AI isn’t the only culprit. You can blame search ads, too. [Search Engine Land]

#7560. Ghost Audiences Are Haunting CTV Measurement

Streaming is officially an advertising business. According to Antenna, nearly half (48%) of all premium subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) accounts in the US were ad-supported in Q1 2026, and 59% of new subscriptions in the quarter were for ad tiers. US ad-supported Premium SVOD subscriptions, meanwhile, hit 110 million by the same quarter, up from 53 million two years prior.

In digital advertising, there is a growing risk of conflating audience size with audience availability. There are now improved ways to think about metrics:

The closer buying moves to the impression, the more costly it becomes to confuse these audiences. Just because a platform’s audience is large doesn’t mean it’s available. And even if it’s available, it isn’t always addressable. The delta between the audience a platform reports on and the audience an advertiser can actually reach is the key gap to close. Consider new viewers who download an app to stream NFL games during the regular season. Samsung Ads recently found that two of every three of these new viewers had “ghosted” the streaming service after the NFL season ended – nearly twice the churn rate of existing users. These ghost audiences remain part of a platform’s reported audience, yet contribute little to campaign-ready inventory. The result is a widening disconnect between reported audience size and the transactable supply advertisers are actually bidding on.

The industry’s next evolution isn’t happening on the demand side – it’s happening closer to the supply. As selling moves closer to the glass, OEMs and SSPs are evolving from distribution partners into intelligence partners, enriching inventory with real-time viewing signals that help determine the value of every impression before it reaches the auction. In that environment, competitive advantage will no longer come from reporting the largest audience. It will come from identifying the best available audience at the exact moment an impression becomes available. The next currency in streaming will be the strongest combination of reach and availability.

#7555. Your Media Plan Might Be Missing Its Best Customers

If you plan media, you’re being asked to find new customers across more screens with fewer partners and to prove that what you’re doing worked. The IAB’s September outlook shows 63% of buyers say acquiring new customers is a top-three goal this year.

But the best media plan is only as good as the data behind it. The limiting factor is often not the sophistication of the targeting tools but what the underlying data can actually reveal. When advertisers rely on the same familiar signals, they risk overlooking valuable audiences that don’t fit their existing definitions.

That’s where carrier data can add a different perspective. By combining insights into mobile app activity with broader patterns of real-world movement, it can uncover connections between consumer behaviors that traditional audience strategies might miss.

Consider a pizza chain trying to acquire new customers. Its media plan might start with people who order from competing pizza restaurants, use pizza delivery apps or exhibit other signals of interest in pizza.

That’s a logical approach to winning market share. But it also assumes that the most valuable prospects are already interested in pizza.

In reality, consumers aren’t always choosing between pizza chains. They’re deciding what type of food they want in the first place. Reaching the right people and understanding what they’re deciding are two different problems.

What happens when you build an audience around that broader decision? Instead of limiting the search to pizza-related signals, marketers can incorporate observed behaviors across restaurant categories, mobile apps and real-world locations. That broader perspective can help identify consumers whose habits and interests make them promising prospects, even if they weren’t included in the original audience definition.

It’s a different way to approach the same marketing objective. Rather than simply refining a model to find more people who fit the presumed target audience, advertisers can use additional evidence to reconsider who belongs in that audience at all.

Advertisers are using T-Mobile carrier data to surface exactly these kinds of audience opportunities.

Take the users of one food delivery app. T-Mobile carrier data shows that this audience is 57% more likely than the national average to also use Gopuff. The audience overindexes on Grubhub and Uber Eats, too. That validates the competitive assumptions most plans start from.

But that same audience is also 45% more likely to be heavy streamers, and overindexes with fantasy sports fans, expectant parents and college students.

Together, these signals suggest an opportunity that a category-focused audience strategy might overlook, such as reaching people during a night in with a show queued up, a game on and dinner handed off to a food delivery app.

That doesn’t mean the data proves these activities are happening together. But it gives advertisers a new hypothesis to explore and potentially new audiences, messages and media placements to test.

A data set that only looks at one category can help find the next pizza order. But looking at data across apps and mobility patterns can reveal a broader range of behaviors and potential new occasions to reach consumers.

The effectiveness of audience modeling depends on the quality and breadth of the signals behind it. Carrier data provides a particularly useful foundation, combining observed app ownership and engagement with patterns of real-world movement and available demographic attributes.

Because consumers carry their phones throughout the day, these signals offer a perspective on behaviors that might otherwise be scattered across different apps, platforms and physical environments. Combining them at the audience level helps advertisers build a more complete understanding of consumer interests and activities without relying on individual-level tracking.

It’s also important to distinguish what’s observed from what’s modeled. Carrier data is observed and deterministic. The scale is modeled.

Platforms such as Blis and Vistar Media use carrier data as a starting point to model and activate audiences across connected TV, audio, mobile and digital out-of-home, including environments where traditional device identifiers aren’t available.

The modeling is only as good as what it starts from, which is why the breadth and quality of observed behavioral signals matter. And while identity still matters, strategies that don’t rely exclusively on any one identifier or platform provide additional resilience as advertising identifiers face continuing restrictions.

For media planners, four questions are worth exploring:

These questions expose a hard truth: A media plan can only be as comprehensive as the view of the consumer it’s built on.

Carrier data is a stronger starting point. Because it draws on observed behavior across apps and location patterns, it can inform more dynamic approaches to reaching customers. With Blis, carrier-informed audiences can be activated across omnichannel media. With Vistar Media, those same audiences can help identify relevant digital out-of-home screens by location, frequency and daypart. This approach can help brands strengthen existing connections and reach new audiences in relevant moments.

Tonight, people across the country will decide what to eat, with plenty of restaurants competing for their attention. Reaching them with a relevant message at the right moment requires more than knowing which restaurants they’ve visited or which apps they use. It requires understanding how their behaviors fit into a broader picture of their interests and habits.

The clearer that picture, the better equipped advertisers are to recognize valuable prospects, including the ones their original audience definitions overlooked.

#7552. Smart Acquisition Or Frankenstack? Stagwell-Freestar And DoorDash-Instacart

It’s fall, and M&A is in the air. Two acquisitions happened this week: Stagwell bought Freestar, and DoorDash agreed to buy Instacart.

Here at AdExchanger, we’re always intrigued by the rationale for acquisitions – from the ones that feel like yin meeting yang to the ones that feel more like stitching together a Frankenstack. (Had to get a spooky reference in!)

In the first half of the podcast, we discuss Stagwell buying Freestar. Why would an indie agency want to build a company that helps open web publishers better set up their ad stacks? Our managing editor, Anthony Vargas, who covered the acquisition, talks about the hints the companies dropped, including how Freestar’s 1,000 publisher site connections could support Stagwell’s principal media business. Are we seeing a rehash of GroupM buying ad network 24/7 Real Media – 19 years later?

Then, when retailers merge, could the extremely fragmented retail media space defragment just a bit? At the time of the recording, DoorDash was in advanced talks to buy Instacart – and on Thursday, news dropped that the acquisition was official.

Pending approval, DoorDash Ads and Instacart’s Carrot Ads will likely come together. Carrot Ads also offers a white-labeled retail media business, which recently added Gopuff as a customer. So imagine Russian nesting dolls, or that image of a whale eating a shark eating a fish – because this type of M&A is going to change how marketers work with retail media companies, which our senior editor, James Hercher, discusses to close out this week.

#7547. Down To The Wire To Acquire; Meta Wants To Be TV, Too

Are we in for a year-ending blockbuster M&A spree?

The Information jokes that CEOs ought to “get your deals in while ya still can, folks.”

A convergence of factors could make for a splashy Q4. As AdExchanger discussed in our Big Story Podcast last week, The Trump administration hasn’t been opposing acquisitions that would have drawn tough scrutiny under the Biden admin. Well, DoorDash CEO Tony Xu confirmed to The Information that he backed out of the company’s previous attempt to buy Instacart in 2021 because he worried Biden-era regulators would squash it.

Another factor in M&A’s favor: Many valuable businesses are struggling with risk-averse investors who don’t know how the AI revolution will shake out. The Information cites Duolingo, Coursera and Zoom as companies that have lost investor support but that would be attractive to buyers. They could join Bumble or Roku in limping to an exit.

Interestingly, what Duolingo, Coursera and Zoom have in common is that they’ve put little effort into earning ad revenue. In 2021, Zoom briefly tested a pilot ad program to monetize free users. That went away a year later.

These companies have the scaled user bases and first-party data assets marketers covet, but not much appetite for the ads biz. Could M&A flip the switch?

If YouTube’s TV, And Meta’s TV, Then Who’s Flying The Plane?

Everyone’s sick of the “Is YouTube TV?” debate. Great news: Now we can argue about whether Meta is TV, instead!

Last week, Meta announced that it’s testing long-form content on Instagram, allowing creators to share content up to 90 minutes long. The announcement comes alongside an influx of CTV spending among direct-to-consumer brands as platforms court midsize advertisers.

Cody Plofker, former CEO and CMO of makeup brand Jones Road, had been against TV advertising until he realized spending 80% of the company budget on Meta was limiting brand exposure, he said at Tatari’s Forward event in New York on Thursday.

Like Jones Road, many DTC brands have “[maxed] out social platforms” and are now putting more focus on TV advertising “as a performance vehicle,” Mike Shields writes in Next in Media.

And CTV ad platforms like Tatari are taking inspiration from Meta and Google by launching their own optimization engines.

Never one to back down from a fight, Meta is searching for its own spot in the TV landscape.

But YouTube is already known for engaged, loyal followings, Shields points out. And YouTube’s content is delivered on demand, which is a fit for TV, whereas Instagram’s algorithmic feed isn’t the traditional TV experience.

As one insider in the creator market tells Shields, why take away what’s working on YouTube TV and redirect resources to Instagram TV?

AI search is the new boogeyman robbing publishers of ad revenue. But another long-feared boogeyman – brand safety – can still spook the sell side.

Last week, former writers for the feminist news site Jezebel raised the alarm that hundreds of articles had been removed from the site. They pointed the finger at Jezebel’s new owner, Paste Magazine, which acquired the publication from G/O Media in 2023.

Anna Merlan, a former Jezebel writer now reporting for Mother Jones, says she heard from sources familiar with Paste that its publisher, William Sagan, decided to remove the articles after an “advertising and analytics company” flagged more than 4,000 articles as “not brand safe.”

But Sagan denied that Paste deleted the articles over brand safety concerns in statements provided to Mother Jones and The Washington Post. He says Paste often flags articles for any number of reasons, including grammatical errors, and temporarily reverts these stories to “draft” status. Indeed, many of the Jezebel articles taken down last week were republished soon after their authors started raising questions.

Paste’s exact motivation for taking the articles down remains unclear. But you can’t blame former Jezebel writers for being sensitive about brand safety.

Jezebel has long suffered monetization troubles tied to advertiser concerns over its coverage. Former Paste editor-in-chief Josh Jackson even claimed he never knew the extent to which brand safety solutions can demonetize publisher content until Paste acquired Jezebel.

Challenger social platforms saw their stock prices drop significantly after reporting Q3 earnings on Thursday. Reddit shares fell 29% and Roblox dropped 17% on Friday due to user growth concerns, while Pinterest dipped 3% after missing ad revenue expectations. [Yahoo Finance]

People Inc. lays off 195 employees, largely in its “print and legacy web businesses,” due to “rapid changes in media,” according to a memo from CEO Neil Vogel. [The Hollywood Reporter]

A network of 37 fake local news websites is boosting mainly Democratic candidates in swing states ahead of the midterm elections – and their content is being picked up by ChatGPT. #7542. AI Labels Don’t Tell Consumers Whether An Ad’s Claims Are Real

Disclosure: Sourin Chakrabarti works on AI labeling for advertising at Meta. The views expressed are his own and do not represent Meta.

In October 2025, three clips appearing to show police detaining and pepper-spraying protesters racked up millions of views across X, Instagram and TikTok. Created with OpenAI’s Sora, the videos carried visible watermarks, yet NewsGuard found that users still cited them as evidence that the events occurred. The footage crossed an unsettling threshold: It didn’t just look realistic; it functioned as visual proof.

Most concern about deepfakes has focused on politics. But the same tactic is now appearing in advertising, where synthetic content can make a product claim look proven.

In a recent campaign investigated by Full Fact, a supposed doctor claiming to be affiliated with Guy’s and St Thomas’ NHS Foundation Trust tested a weight-loss patch and appeared to grow thinner on camera. The trust called the posts “completely fraudulent,” while Google’s Gemini detected SynthID watermarks confirming AI involvement. Yet that watermark only revealed that AI was involved, not where the fiction ended. Was only the doctor’s face synthetic? Or were the medical authority, hospital connection, personal experience and physical transformation invented, too?

This exposes the fundamental blind spot of AI disclosures: they flag the production tool, not the illusion. A generic label tells consumers that AI was used to build an ad, but leaves them to guess where reality ends and fiction begins.

The fraudulent NHS weight-loss ad was not an isolated incident. In 2025, the Australian Medical Association warned that deepfakes impersonating prominent doctors were promoting unproven products, with clinicians discovering the fraud only when patients asked whether to swap prescribed treatments for advertised miracle cures. In 2026, Chinese regulators launched an enforcement campaign targeting businesses that mass-produced fabricated consumer-experience posts.

The legal principle predates generative AI. In FTC v. Colgate-Palmolive Co., a shaving cream commercial used a plexiglass prop in place of real sandpaper. Viewers were misled because the simulation was presented as a genuine product test. The case offers a useful test for AI advertising today: Does an ad merely illustrate a claim or does it ask viewers to treat a synthetic scene as real-world proof?

Platforms and regulators are building substantial disclosure systems to track synthetic content. Google displays “How this ad was made” panels, Meta attaches “AI info” labels and TikTok offers “AIGC” self-disclosure controls. Governments are pushing in the same direction: The European Union’s Article 50 rules require transparency for synthetic media, China mandates explicit AI markers and New York requires advertisements to identify synthetic performers.

Yet current AI-labeling systems mostly tell consumers that AI was used, not what it changed or why it matters. The same label can appear on an ad with a decorative AI background and one with an entirely fabricated testimonial. Those uses are not equally misleading, but a generic label may not distinguish between them.

Some policies address the clearest cases. The Advertising Standards Council of India’s 2026 draft guidance identifies fabricated experts, endorsements and exaggerated results as high-risk uses that labeling alone cannot fix. TikTok Shop prohibits AI-generated professional identities used to sell health products and alterations that misrepresent product performance. But a harder question remains: What about AI simulations that are lawful but could still be mistaken for real-world evidence?

The disclosure gap is becoming urgent as AI ad generation reaches industrial scale. In 2025, advertisers created three times as many Gemini-generated assets on Google as in 2024, including nearly 70 million in the final quarter alone. Meta has reportedly aimed to automate ad creation and targeting with AI by the end of 2026. Because these tools are embedded directly into ad-creation systems, safeguards cannot rely on post hoc consumer complaints. They must operate systematically across millions of ads.

The answer is not to label every synthetic pixel. Building on the IAB’s January 2026 disclosure framework, regulators should adopt a risk-based approach requiring specific disclosures whenever AI material appears to provide evidence for a product claim. This approach would produce three outcomes:

Platforms could implement this approach by requiring advertisers to disclose three things: the role played by any AI-created person or scene, whether the generated material depicts product performance or results and what real-world evidence supports the claim. Meta, Google and TikTok already accept advertiser declarations, so these questions could fit into existing workflows. Platforms should also retain a record of the advertiser’s answers and the notice shown to consumers, creating an auditable trail of how each ad was reviewed and presented. An emerging industry proposal calls this a served disclosure receipt.

Consider the weight-loss patch video. Under this system, an “AI was used” label would be only the starting point. The advertiser would have to identify the doctor as a synthetic expert, classify the apparent transformation as a product-performance claim and clarify whether the testimonial represented a real customer. It would also have to provide evidence supporting the weight-loss claim. If the doctor was falsely presented as real, the testimonial was fabricated or the result lacked substantiation, the ad would not be approved.

The goal is labels that answer the question consumers actually face: not just whether AI made the ad but whether AI made up the reason to buy.

“Data-Driven Thinking” is written by members of the media community and contains fresh ideas on the digital revolution in media.

#7536. Fox Doesn’t Want To Talk About Roku, But It’s Got Lots To Say About Tubi And Politics

Any investor hoping to ask about Fox’s pending Roku acquisition during its fiscal Q1 2027 earnings call on Monday was out of luck.

Fox’s IR rep made that clear up front and pointed analysts to Fox’s SEC filings instead.

However, CEO Lachlan Murdoch did share a mini update, including that shareholder and foreign regulatory approvals are in, although Fox is still working with the DOJ on antitrust clearance.

“[We] expect to close the transaction as soon as we can,” Murdoch told investors, noting that Fox’s “conviction in the opportunity has only grown.” Pairing Roku’s platform with Fox’s sports, news and entertainment content is a good recipe for building “our position in the fastest-growing segments of the media landscape,” he said.

Fox’s revenue rose 22% to $4.6 billion in the quarter, including a 47% jump in advertising revenue (60% in its TV segment) driven by the World Cup, early midterm spending and Tubi, its free ad-supported streaming service.

Tubi grew revenue 35% year over year, alongside a 23% uptick in total view time.

Fox attributed that engagement to a combo of Tubi’s content library, 10 new originals and a World Cup hub, which drew on Fox’s US English-language rights to the tournament.

Tubi also got a boost from viral content from more than 600 creators. Its Tubi for Creators program launched in 2025 with six creators and has since wooed big YouTube names like MrBeast and Jomboy Media.

And profits are growing, too, despite higher content costs, according to CFO Steve Tomsic, who noted that Tubi is contributing more to the bottom line than it was in the year-ago quarter when it turned its first profit – a development Murdoch himself apparently didn’t see coming.

A Bank of America analyst on the call reminded Murdoch that a year or so ago he’d said that Tubi’s growth, then in the midteens, wouldn’t be sustainable.

“I don’t remember saying that, but I’m sure I did … Thank you for calling me out on that one,” Murdoch said, adding that Tubi’s profit margins should settle in the 20% range once it reaches “further maturity.”

Advertising is the main engine behind Tubi’s momentum, which Murdoch said is continuing into the current quarter. Tubi’s audience is young, diverse and mostly cord-free, he said, which is like catnip for advertisers.

“They’re a very hard market for advertisers to reach,” he said, which, in a midterm year, is a pretty good pitch to political campaigns.

Fox booked more than $350 million in political ads this cycle, and Tubi was responsible for roughly $50 million of that.

Most of the rest – $250 million-plus – went to Fox’s local stations, including many in battleground states, where demand is so high that some stations run out of ad inventory. The remaining $50-ish million went to political ads across national sports, news and entertainment.

But if you squint, and not that hard, Tubi also kind of counts as local advertising in Murdoch’s view. “It’s effectively local revenue because it’s targeted,” he said.

Politics aside, sports has been a tailwind, too.

The FIFA World Cup final was the most-watched soccer telecast in US history; the World Series, which aired on Fox, averaged 12 million viewers; and Fox’s NFL “America’s Game of the Week” is drawing an average of nearly 25 million viewers per game.

But Murdoch was also careful to temper expectations for Fox One, Fox’s streaming service for Fox content.

It’s not like there’s a World Cup every year – or a midterm election.

“It’s always a point in time,” Murdoch said. “Every couple years, you’ve got to be careful to understand the strength of the political cycle.”

And not everything at Fox was a win this past quarter, no matter how you spin it.

Fox News finished its fiscal Q1 as the most-watched cable news network, with 2.1 million primetime viewers and 1.3 million across all dayparts. But those figures were down 17% and 16% year over year, according to Nielsen, and Fox News was the only major cable news network to see declines. The slide has continued into October, when total-day ratings fell 27% ahead of the midterms.

Murdoch blamed tough comps against last year’s “tremendous news cycle,” which included the inauguration, Charlie Kirk’s assassination and DOGE-related drama. He compared this cycle to the 2006 midterms, when a second-term president was halfway through his term.

It’s not that viewers are defecting to CNN or MS Now, he said. They’re “just fatigued and watching slightly less television overall.” (Even so, Nielsen does show CNN and MS Now both up from last year.)

Meanwhile, cable advertising rose 8%, helped along by sports, but digital news ad revenue fell. Asked about that – we mourn you preemptively, open web – Murdoch pointed to Fox News Digital’s standing as the top news site in the US and called digital news a “hyper-competitive market.”
